Below is a side-by-side breakdown of Tomorrow.io, Google Weather API, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, and Weatherbit across pricing, latency, nowcast horizon, and coverage.\n\n## Pricing Tiers Compared\n\n| API | Free Tier | Entry Paid Tier | Mid Tier | High Volume/Enterprise |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 500 calls/day, 3 req/s, 5-day forecast, 1 location/alert[1] | Team ~$23/mo, ~7,500 calls/day[2] | Business ~$120/mo, ~3M calls/day[2] | Custom (Gridline, premium layers, minutely resolution, 14-day horizon)[3][2] |\n| Google Weather API | 10,000 calls/month free[4] | $0.15/1,000 calls (10k\u2013100k)[4] | Tiered down to $0.06/1,000 calls (1M\u20135M)[4] | $0.038/1,000 calls (5M+)[4] |\n| Visual Crossing | 1,000 records/day free forever[5] | Professional $35/mo (10M records/mo)[6] | Corporate $150/mo (unlimited, fair use)[6] | Custom Enterprise (SLA, concurrency, licensing)[7] |\n| Open-Meteo | 10,000 calls/day non-commercial, no key[8][9] | API Standard $29/mo (1M calls/mo)[9] | API Professional $99/mo (5M calls/mo)[9] | Enterprise custom (50M+ calls)[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 50 requests/day, non-commercial only[10] | Standard $40\u201345/mo (25,000 req/day)[11][12] | Plus $180\u2013195/mo (250,000 req/day)[11][10] | Business $475/mo (2M req/day); Enterprise custom ~$950+/mo[11][10] |\n\nVisual Crossing and Open-Meteo stand out for pricing transparency, billing per record or per call at fixed, published rates rather than requiring a sales call. Tomorrow.io's most valuable capabilities, including premium data layers and true minutely nowcasting, remain gated behind a \"contact sales\" wall, which makes total cost harder to estimate upfront compared to the other four. Google's tier is unusual in this group in that it is consumption-based only, with no fixed monthly subscription option, and it just exited a $0-cost preview period.[7][2][4][13][1][9]\n\n## Latency Benchmarks\n\n| API | Typical Response Time | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Open-Meteo | Under 10 ms (single location, vendor-claimed); ~289\u2013717 ms observed in third-party tests | NVMe columnar storage; vendor cites sub-10ms, but independent probes show ~300-700ms depending on route[14][15][16] |\n| Visual Crossing | Not independently benchmarked in detail; offers a low-latency \"Timeline LLX\" API tier | Optimized tier exists specifically for apps needing very low response times[17] |\n| Tomorrow.io | ~110-125 ms typical; briefly degraded to 429 errors during an August 2026 incident | Third-party uptime monitor recorded a 7-hour degradation event[18] |\n| Google Weather API | Not independently benchmarked; refresh cadence 15-30 min | Rate limit of 6,000 queries/minute by default[19] |\n| Weatherbit | Not independently benchmarked | Enterprise tier advertises a 200ms response SLA[11] |\n\nOpen-Meteo is architecturally built for speed, storing ","final":false},"document_review":null,"screenshot":null,"slide_file":null,"audio_file":null,"model_3d":null,"asset_diff":null,"external_url":null,"visualization":null,"teammate_task":null,"pull_request":null,"session":null,"teammate_worker":null,"automation":null,"download_info":[],"preview_info":null,"version_info":null,"fallback_info":{"name":"","webview_url":"","preview_image_url":null},"is_primary_asset":true,"backend_uuid_slug":null,"parent_asset_id":null,"root_asset_id":null,"created_at":null,"annotation":null}]}]

Below is a side-by-side breakdown of Tomorrow.io, Google Weather API, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, and Weatherbit across pricing, latency, nowcast horizon, and coverage.\n\n## Pricing Tiers Compared\n\n| API | Free Tier | Entry Paid Tier | Mid Tier | High Volume/Enterprise |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 500 calls/day, 3 req/s, 5-day forecast, 1 location/alert[1] | Team ~$23/mo, ~7,500 calls/day[2] | Business ~$120/mo, ~3M calls/day[2] | Custom (Gridline, premium layers, minutely resolution, 14-day horizon)[3][2] |\n| Google Weather API | 10,000 calls/month free[4] | $0.15/1,000 calls (10k\u2013100k)[4] | Tiered down to $0.06/1,000 calls (1M\u20135M)[4] | $0.038/1,000 calls (5M+)[4] |\n| Visual Crossing | 1,000 records/day free forever[5] | Professional $35/mo (10M records/mo)[6] | Corporate $150/mo (unlimited, fair use)[6] | Custom Enterprise (SLA, concurrency, licensing)[7] |\n| Open-Meteo | 10,000 calls/day non-commercial, no key[8][9] | API Standard $29/mo (1M calls/mo)[9] | API Professional $99/mo (5M calls/mo)[9] | Enterprise custom (50M+ calls)[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 50 requests/day, non-commercial only[10] | Standard $40\u201345/mo (25,000 req/day)[11][12] | Plus $180\u2013195/mo (250,000 req/day)[11][10] | Business $475/mo (2M req/day); Enterprise custom ~$950+/mo[11][10] |\n\nVisual Crossing and Open-Meteo stand out for pricing transparency, billing per record or per call at fixed, published rates rather than requiring a sales call. Tomorrow.io's most valuable capabilities, including premium data layers and true minutely nowcasting, remain gated behind a \"contact sales\" wall, which makes total cost harder to estimate upfront compared to the other four. Google's tier is unusual in this group in that it is consumption-based only, with no fixed monthly subscription option, and it just exited a $0-cost preview period.[7][2][4][13][1][9]\n\n## Latency Benchmarks\n\n| API | Typical Response Time | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Open-Meteo | Under 10 ms (single location, vendor-claimed); ~289\u2013717 ms observed in third-party tests | NVMe columnar storage; vendor cites sub-10ms, but independent probes show ~300-700ms depending on route[14][15][16] |\n| Visual Crossing | Not independently benchmarked in detail; offers a low-latency \"Timeline LLX\" API tier | Optimized tier exists specifically for apps needing very low response times[17] |\n| Tomorrow.io | ~110-125 ms typical; briefly degraded to 429 errors during an August 2026 incident | Third-party uptime monitor recorded a 7-hour degradation event[18] |\n| Google Weather API | Not independently benchmarked; refresh cadence 15-30 min | Rate limit of 6,000 queries/minute by default[19] |\n| Weatherbit | Not independently benchmarked | Enterprise tier advertises a 200ms response SLA[11] |\n\nOpen-Meteo is architecturally built for speed, storing time-series data on NVMe disks specifically to minimize per-call latency, though real-world third-party measurements land closer to a few hundred milliseconds rather than the vendor's sub-10ms marketing figure. Only Weatherbit explicitly guarantees a latency SLA (200ms) and only on its priciest Enterprise plan.[11][14][16]\n\n## Nowcasting Horizon and Radar Capability\n\n| API | Nowcast Horizon | Update Frequency | Radar/Data Source |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 60-minute minute-by-minute precipitation (premium/Enterprise only)[20][21] | Radar+satellite composite refreshes every 5 minutes; proprietary \"UP\" blend refreshes every 30 seconds[22][23] | Proprietary microsatellite radar constellation + 1,000+ ground radar stations, 2.5km resolution[24][21] |\n| Google Weather API | 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast (Experimental endpoint)[25] | Current/hourly data refreshed every 15-30 minutes[26][27] | Google explicitly states it does not do true nowcast/minute forecasting via traditional radar; the minute endpoint is AI-model based[19] |\n| Visual Crossing | Minute-by-minute precipitation timing \"when available\" within its Weather Forecast Live tool[17] | Standard 15-day forecast; not a dedicated short-interval radar product[5] | Not radar-native; interpolation-based hyperlocal modeling[28] |\n| Open-Meteo | 15-minutely data (Central Europe and North America only); hourly elsewhere via interpolation[8] | High-res regional models (ICON-D2, HRRR, AROME) update every 1-3 hours; global models every 6 hours[14] | No true radar-based nowcasting; model data only, no station observations[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 60-minute minutely rain/snow nowcast[29][12] | Included from the Standard paid tier upward (not on Free)[11][30] | Blends stations, radar, and satellite globally[29] |\n\nTomorrow.io has the most genuinely radar-driven, sub-hour nowcast product in this group, with a proprietary satellite radar constellation designed to fill gaps where ground radar coverage is poor, and refresh rates as tight as 30 seconds to 5 minutes. Weatherbit offers a comparable 60-minute minutely product but only unlocks it once you leave the free tier. Google explicitly disclaims traditional nowcasting and instead offers an AI-modeled 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast as an experimental endpoint, not classic radar extrapolation. Open-Meteo is the weakest here since it is pure numerical-model data with no radar ingestion, so true \"rain starting in X minutes\" nowcasting is out of scope.[12][25][24][19][22][23][9][11]\n\n## Geographic Coverage\n\n| API | Coverage Notes |\n|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | Global coverage claimed via NextGen satellite network, specifically marketed as filling North American radar gaps (27% of US landmass previously had poor radar quality)[24] |\n| Google Weather API | Global except Japan, Korea (alerts-only), and a short list of excluded countries (China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria); initial launch also excludes remote unpopulated areas like open ocean and deserts[4][13][19] |\n| Visual Crossing | Global coverage for ","final":false},"document_review":null,"screenshot":null,"slide_file":null,"audio_file":null,"model_3d":null,"asset_diff":null,"external_url":null,"visualization":null,"teammate_task":null,"pull_request":null,"session":null,"teammate_worker":null,"automation":null,"download_info":[],"preview_info":null,"version_info":null,"fallback_info":{"name":"","webview_url":"","preview_image_url":null},"is_primary_asset":true,"backend_uuid_slug":null,"parent_asset_id":null,"root_asset_id":null,"created_at":null,"annotation":null}]}]

Below is a side-by-side breakdown of Tomorrow.io, Google Weather API, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, and Weatherbit across pricing, latency, nowcast horizon, and coverage.\n\n## Pricing Tiers Compared\n\n| API | Free Tier | Entry Paid Tier | Mid Tier | High Volume/Enterprise |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 500 calls/day, 3 req/s, 5-day forecast, 1 location/alert[1] | Team ~$23/mo, ~7,500 calls/day[2] | Business ~$120/mo, ~3M calls/day[2] | Custom (Gridline, premium layers, minutely resolution, 14-day horizon)[3][2] |\n| Google Weather API | 10,000 calls/month free[4] | $0.15/1,000 calls (10k\u2013100k)[4] | Tiered down to $0.06/1,000 calls (1M\u20135M)[4] | $0.038/1,000 calls (5M+)[4] |\n| Visual Crossing | 1,000 records/day free forever[5] | Professional $35/mo (10M records/mo)[6] | Corporate $150/mo (unlimited, fair use)[6] | Custom Enterprise (SLA, concurrency, licensing)[7] |\n| Open-Meteo | 10,000 calls/day non-commercial, no key[8][9] | API Standard $29/mo (1M calls/mo)[9] | API Professional $99/mo (5M calls/mo)[9] | Enterprise custom (50M+ calls)[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 50 requests/day, non-commercial only[10] | Standard $40\u201345/mo (25,000 req/day)[11][12] | Plus $180\u2013195/mo (250,000 req/day)[11][10] | Business $475/mo (2M req/day); Enterprise custom ~$950+/mo[11][10] |\n\nVisual Crossing and Open-Meteo stand out for pricing transparency, billing per record or per call at fixed, published rates rather than requiring a sales call. Tomorrow.io's most valuable capabilities, including premium data layers and true minutely nowcasting, remain gated behind a \"contact sales\" wall, which makes total cost harder to estimate upfront compared to the other four. Google's tier is unusual in this group in that it is consumption-based only, with no fixed monthly subscription option, and it just exited a $0-cost preview period.[7][2][4][13][1][9]\n\n## Latency Benchmarks\n\n| API | Typical Response Time | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Open-Meteo | Under 10 ms (single location, vendor-claimed); ~289\u2013717 ms observed in third-party tests | NVMe columnar storage; vendor cites sub-10ms, but independent probes show ~300-700ms depending on route[14][15][16] |\n| Visual Crossing | Not independently benchmarked in detail; offers a low-latency \"Timeline LLX\" API tier | Optimized tier exists specifically for apps needing very low response times[17] |\n| Tomorrow.io | ~110-125 ms typical; briefly degraded to 429 errors during an August 2026 incident | Third-party uptime monitor recorded a 7-hour degradation event[18] |\n| Google Weather API | Not independently benchmarked; refresh cadence 15-30 min | Rate limit of 6,000 queries/minute by default[19] |\n| Weatherbit | Not independently benchmarked | Enterprise tier advertises a 200ms response SLA[11] |\n\nOpen-Meteo is architecturally built for speed, storing time-series data on NVMe disks specifically to minimize per-call latency, though real-world third-party measurements land closer to a few hundred milliseconds rather than the vendor's sub-10ms marketing figure. Only Weatherbit explicitly guarantees a latency SLA (200ms) and only on its priciest Enterprise plan.[11][14][16]\n\n## Nowcasting Horizon and Radar Capability\n\n| API | Nowcast Horizon | Update Frequency | Radar/Data Source |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 60-minute minute-by-minute precipitation (premium/Enterprise only)[20][21] | Radar+satellite composite refreshes every 5 minutes; proprietary \"UP\" blend refreshes every 30 seconds[22][23] | Proprietary microsatellite radar constellation + 1,000+ ground radar stations, 2.5km resolution[24][21] |\n| Google Weather API | 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast (Experimental endpoint)[25] | Current/hourly data refreshed every 15-30 minutes[26][27] | Google explicitly states it does not do true nowcast/minute forecasting via traditional radar; the minute endpoint is AI-model based[19] |\n| Visual Crossing | Minute-by-minute precipitation timing \"when available\" within its Weather Forecast Live tool[17] | Standard 15-day forecast; not a dedicated short-interval radar product[5] | Not radar-native; interpolation-based hyperlocal modeling[28] |\n| Open-Meteo | 15-minutely data (Central Europe and North America only); hourly elsewhere via interpolation[8] | High-res regional models (ICON-D2, HRRR, AROME) update every 1-3 hours; global models every 6 hours[14] | No true radar-based nowcasting; model data only, no station observations[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 60-minute minutely rain/snow nowcast[29][12] | Included from the Standard paid tier upward (not on Free)[11][30] | Blends stations, radar, and satellite globally[29] |\n\nTomorrow.io has the most genuinely radar-driven, sub-hour nowcast product in this group, with a proprietary satellite radar constellation designed to fill gaps where ground radar coverage is poor, and refresh rates as tight as 30 seconds to 5 minutes. Weatherbit offers a comparable 60-minute minutely product but only unlocks it once you leave the free tier. Google explicitly disclaims traditional nowcasting and instead offers an AI-modeled 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast as an experimental endpoint, not classic radar extrapolation. Open-Meteo is the weakest here since it is pure numerical-model data with no radar ingestion, so true \"rain starting in X minutes\" nowcasting is out of scope.[12][25][24][19][22][23][9][11]\n\n## Geographic Coverage\n\n| API | Coverage Notes |\n|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | Global coverage claimed via NextGen satellite network, specifically marketed as filling North American radar gaps (27% of US landmass previously had poor radar quality)[24] |\n| Google Weather API | Global except Japan, Korea (alerts-only), and a short list of excluded countries (China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria); initial launch also excludes remote unpopulated areas like open ocean and deserts[4][13][19] |\n| Visual Crossing | Global coverage for both forecast and 50+ years of historical data[31] |\n| Open-Meteo | Global, with highest resolution (1-2 km) in Central Europe, France, Switzerland, UK, and North America; 9-11 km elsewhere[14][9] |\n| Weatherbit | Global coverage blending stations, radar, and satellite[29] |\n\nGoogle is notably the most restrictive on paper, excluding a handful of countries outright and still ramping up quality in remote/unpopulated regions as of its post-GA rollout. Tomorrow.io and Open-Meteo both explicitly engineer around the reality that ground radar is unevenly distributed worldwide, but they solve it differently: Tomorrow.io launches its own radar satellites, while Open-Meteo simply uses the best available numerical model per region without radar at all.[13][14][24][19]\n\n## Practical Takeaways\n\n- **Best true nowcasting**: Tomorrow.io, Below is a side-by-side breakdown of Tomorrow.io, Google Weather API, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, and Weatherbit across pricing, latency, nowcast horizon, and coverage.\n\n## Pricing Tiers Compared\n\n| API | Free Tier | Entry Paid Tier | Mid Tier | High Volume/Enterprise |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 500 calls/day, 3 req/s, 5-day forecast, 1 location/alert[1] | Team ~$23/mo, ~7,500 calls/day[2] | Business ~$120/mo, ~3M calls/day[2] | Custom (Gridline, premium layers, minutely resolution, 14-day horizon)[3][2] |\n| Google Weather API | 10,000 calls/month free[4] | $0.15/1,000 calls (10k\u2013100k)[4] | Tiered down to $0.06/1,000 calls (1M\u20135M)[4] | $0.038/1,000 calls (5M+)[4] |\n| Visual Crossing | 1,000 records/day free forever[5] | Professional $35/mo (10M records/mo)[6] | Corporate $150/mo (unlimited, fair use)[6] | Custom Enterprise (SLA, concurrency, licensing)[7] |\n| Open-Meteo | 10,000 calls/day non-commercial, no key[8][9] | API Standard $29/mo (1M calls/mo)[9] | API Professional $99/mo (5M calls/mo)[9] | Enterprise custom (50M+ calls)[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 50 requests/day, non-commercial only[10] | Standard $40\u201345/mo (25,000 req/day)[11][12] | Plus $180\u2013195/mo (250,000 req/day)[11][10] | Business $475/mo (2M req/day); Enterprise custom ~$950+/mo[11][10] |\n\nVisual Crossing and Open-Meteo stand out for pricing transparency, billing per record or per call at fixed, published rates rather than requiring a sales call. Tomorrow.io's most valuable capabilities, including premium data layers and true minutely nowcasting, remain gated behind a \"contact sales\" wall, which makes total cost harder to estimate upfront compared to the other four. Google's tier is unusual in this group in that it is consumption-based only, with no fixed monthly subscription option, and it just exited a $0-cost preview period.[7][2][4][13][1][9]\n\n## Latency Benchmarks\n\n| API | Typical Response Time | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Open-Meteo | Under 10 ms (single location, vendor-claimed); ~289\u2013717 ms observed in third-party tests | NVMe columnar storage; vendor cites sub-10ms, but independent probes show ~300-700ms depending on route[14][15][16] |\n| Visual Crossing | Not independently benchmarked in detail; offers a low-latency \"Timeline LLX\" API tier | Optimized tier exists specifically for apps needing very low response times[17] |\n| Tomorrow.io | ~110-125 ms typical; briefly degraded to 429 errors during an August 2026 incident | Third-party uptime monitor recorded a 7-hour degradation event[18] |\n| Google Weather API | Not independently benchmarked; refresh cadence 15-30 min | Rate limit of 6,000 queries/minute by default[19] |\n| Weatherbit | Not independently benchmarked | Enterprise tier advertises a 200ms response SLA[11] |\n\nOpen-Meteo is architecturally built for speed, storing time-series data on NVMe disks specifically to minimize per-call latency, though real-world third-party measurements land closer to a few hundred milliseconds rather than the vendor's sub-10ms marketing figure. Only Weatherbit explicitly guarantees a latency SLA (200ms) and only on its priciest Enterprise plan.[11][14][16]\n\n## Nowcasting Horizon and Radar Capability\n\n| API | Nowcast Horizon | Update Frequency | Radar/Data Source |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 60-minute minute-by-minute precipitation (premium/Enterprise only)[20][21] | Radar+satellite composite refreshes every 5 minutes; proprietary \"UP\" blend refreshes every 30 seconds[22][23] | Proprietary microsatellite radar constellation + 1,000+ ground radar stations, 2.5km resolution[24][21] |\n| Google Weather API | 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast (Experimental endpoint)[25] | Current/hourly data refreshed every 15-30 minutes[26][27] | Google explicitly states it does not do true nowcast/minute forecasting via traditional radar; the minute endpoint is AI-model based[19] |\n| Visual Crossing | Minute-by-minute precipitation timing \"when available\" within its Weather Forecast Live tool[17] | Standard 15-day forecast; not a dedicated short-interval radar product[5] | Not radar-native; interpolation-based hyperlocal modeling[28] |\n| Open-Meteo | 15-minutely data (Central Europe and North America only); hourly elsewhere via interpolation[8] | High-res regional models (ICON-D2, HRRR, AROME) update every 1-3 hours; global models every 6 hours[14] | No true radar-based nowcasting; model data only, no station observations[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 60-minute minutely rain/snow nowcast[29][12] | Included from the Standard paid tier upward (not on Free)[11][30] | Blends stations, radar, and satellite globally[29] |\n\nTomorrow.io has the most genuinely radar-driven, sub-hour nowcast product in this group, with a proprietary satellite radar constellation designed to fill gaps where ground radar coverage is poor, and refresh rates as tight as 30 seconds to 5 minutes. Weatherbit offers a comparable 60-minute minutely product but only unlocks it once you leave the free tier. Google explicitly disclaims traditional nowcasting and instead offers an AI-modeled 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast as an experimental endpoint, not classic radar extrapolation. Open-Meteo is the weakest here since it is pure numerical-model data with no radar ingestion, so true \"rain starting in X minutes\" nowcasting is out of scope.[12][25][24][19][22][23][9][11]\n\n## Geographic Coverage\n\n| API | Coverage Notes |\n|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | Global coverage claimed via NextGen satellite network, specifically marketed as filling North American radar gaps (27% of US landmass previously had poor radar quality)[24] |\n| Google Weather API | Global except Japan, Korea (alerts-only), and a short list of excluded countries (China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria); initial launch also excludes remote unpopulated areas like open ocean and deserts[4][13][19] |\n| Visual Crossing | Global coverage for both forecast and 50+ years of historical data[31] |\n| Open-Meteo | Global, with highest resolution (1-2 km) in Central Europe, France, Switzerland, UK, and North America; 9-11 km elsewhere[14][9] |\n| Weatherbit | Global coverage blending stations, radar, and satellite[29] |\n\nGoogle is notably the most restrictive on paper, excluding a handful of countries outright and still ramping up quality in remote/unpopulated regions as of its post-GA rollout. Tomorrow.io and Open-Meteo both explicitly engineer around the reality that ground radar is unevenly distributed worldwide, but they solve it differently: Tomorrow.io launches its own radar Below is a side-by-side breakdown of Tomorrow.io, Google Weather API, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, and Weatherbit across pricing, latency, nowcast horizon, and coverage.\n\n## Pricing Tiers Compared\n\n| API | Free Tier | Entry Paid Tier | Mid Tier | High Volume/Enterprise |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Tomorrow.io | 500 calls/day, 3 req/s, 5-day forecast, 1 location/alert[1] | Team ~$23/mo, ~7,500 calls/day[2] | Business ~$120/mo, ~3M calls/day[2] | Custom (Gridline, premium layers, minutely resolution, 14-day horizon)[3][2] |\n| Google Weather API | 10,000 calls/month free[4] | $0.15/1,000 calls (10k\u2013100k)[4] | Tiered down to $0.06/1,000 calls (1M\u20135M)[4] | $0.038/1,000 calls (5M+)[4] |\n| Visual Crossing | 1,000 records/day free forever[5] | Professional $35/mo (10M records/mo)[6] | Corporate $150/mo (unlimited, fair use)[6] | Custom Enterprise (SLA, concurrency, licensing)[7] |\n| Open-Meteo | 10,000 calls/day non-commercial, no key[8][9] | API Standard $29/mo (1M calls/mo)[9] | API Professional $99/mo (5M calls/mo)[9] | Enterprise custom (50M+ calls)[9] |\n| Weatherbit | 50 requests/day, non-commercial only[10] | Standard $40\u201345/mo (25,000 req/day)[11][12] | Plus $180\u2013195/mo (250,000 req/day)[11][10] | Business $475/mo (2M req/day); Enterprise custom ~$950+/mo[11][10] |\n\nVisual Crossing and Open-Meteo stand out for pricing transparency, billing per record or per call at fixed, published rates rather than requiring a sales call. Tomorrow.io's most valuable capabilities, including premium data layers and true minutely nowcasting, remain gated behind a \"contact sales\" wall, which makes total cost harder to estimate upfront compared to the other four. Google's tier is unusual in this group in that it is consumption-based only, with no fixed monthly subscription option, and it just exited a $0-cost preview period.[7][2][4][13][1][9]\n\n## Latency Benchmarks\n\n| API | Typical Response Time | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Open-Meteo | Under 10 ms (single location, vendor-claimed); ~289\u2013717 ms observed in third-party tests | NVMe columnar storage; vendor cites sub-10ms, but independent probes show ~300-700ms depending on route[14][15][16] |\n| Visual Crossing | Not independently benchmarked in detail; offers a low-latency \"Timeline LLX\" API tier | Optimized tier exists specifically for apps needing very low response times[17] |\n| Tomorrow.io | ~110-125 ms typical; briefly degraded to 429 errors during an August 2026 incident | Third-party uptime monitor recorded a 7-hour degradation event[18] |\n| Google Weather API | Not independently benchmarked; refresh cadence 15-30 min | Rate limit of 6,000 queries/minute by default[19] |\n| Weatherbit | Not independently benchmarked | Enterprise tier advertises a 200ms response SLA[11] |\n\nOpen-Meteo is architecturally built for speed, storing time-series data on NVMe disks specifically to minimize per-call latency, though real-world third-party measurements land closer to a few hundred milliseconds rather than the vendor's sub-10ms marketing figure. I've compiled a detailed comparison of Tomorrow.io, Google Weather API, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, and Weatherbit across pricing, latency, nowcast horizon, and geographic coverage.

**Key highlights:**
- **Pricing**: Open-Meteo and Visual Crossing offer the most transparent, self-serve pricing; Tomorrow.io's best features require a sales conversation.
- **Latency**: Open-Meteo is architecturally the fastest (though real-world benchmarks show ~300-700ms vs. its sub-10ms marketing claim); Weatherbit's Enterprise tier is the only one with a published latency SLA.
- **Nowcast horizon**: Tomorrow.io leads with proprietary radar/satellite blending refreshed every 30 seconds to 5 minutes; Google explicitly doesn't do traditional radar-based nowcasting, opting for a 6-hour AI-modeled minute forecast instead; Open-Meteo has no radar-based nowcasting at all.
- **Coverage**: Google is the most restrictive (excludes several countries outright), while Tomorrow.io and Open-Meteo both engineer around uneven ground-radar coverage globally, just via different approaches (satellites vs. model-only).

The full report includes detailed pricing tables, latency benchmarks, and a practical takeaways section matched to different use cases.

research_answer_content.title: Weather Nowcasting API Comparison: Tomorrow.io, Google, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, Weatherbit

research_report.name: Weather Nowcasting API Comparison: Tomorrow.io, Google, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, Weatherbit
research_report.source_content:
Weather nowcasting APIs vary widely in cost structure, raw response speed, how far ahead they can predict short-term precipitation, and where in the world they actually work well. Below is a side-by-side breakdown of Tomorrow.io, Google Weather API, Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo, and Weatherbit across pricing, latency, nowcast horizon, and coverage.

## Pricing Tiers Compared

| API | Free Tier | Entry Paid Tier | Mid Tier | High Volume/Enterprise |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tomorrow.io | 500 calls/day, 3 req/s, 5-day forecast, 1 location/alert[1] | Team ~$23/mo, ~7,500 calls/day[2] | Business ~$120/mo, ~3M calls/day[2] | Custom (Gridline, premium layers, minutely resolution, 14-day horizon)[3][2] |
| Google Weather API | 10,000 calls/month free[4] | $0.15/1,000 calls (10k–100k)[4] | Tiered down to $0.06/1,000 calls (1M–5M)[4] | $0.038/1,000 calls (5M+)[4] |
| Visual Crossing | 1,000 records/day free forever[5] | Professional $35/mo (10M records/mo)[6] | Corporate $150/mo (unlimited, fair use)[6] | Custom Enterprise (SLA, concurrency, licensing)[7] |
| Open-Meteo | 10,000 calls/day non-commercial, no key[8][9] | API Standard $29/mo (1M calls/mo)[9] | API Professional $99/mo (5M calls/mo)[9] | Enterprise custom (50M+ calls)[9] |
| Weatherbit | 50 requests/day, non-commercial only[10] | Standard $40–45/mo (25,000 req/day)[11][12] | Plus $180–195/mo (250,000 req/day)[11][10] | Business $475/mo (2M req/day); Enterprise custom ~$950+/mo[11][10] |

Visual Crossing and Open-Meteo stand out for pricing transparency, billing per record or per call at fixed, published rates rather than requiring a sales call. Tomorrow.io's most valuable capabilities, including premium data layers and true minutely nowcasting, remain gated behind a "contact sales" wall, which makes total cost harder to estimate upfront compared to the other four. Google's tier is unusual in this group in that it is consumption-based only, with no fixed monthly subscription option, and it just exited a $0-cost preview period.[7][2][4][13][1][9]

## Latency Benchmarks

| API | Typical Response Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Open-Meteo | Under 10 ms (single location, vendor-claimed); ~289–717 ms observed in third-party tests | NVMe columnar storage; vendor cites sub-10ms, but independent probes show ~300-700ms depending on route[14][15][16] |
| Visual Crossing | Not independently benchmarked in detail; offers a low-latency "Timeline LLX" API tier | Optimized tier exists specifically for apps needing very low response times[17] |
| Tomorrow.io | ~110-125 ms typical; briefly degraded to 429 errors during an August 2026 incident | Third-party uptime monitor recorded a 7-hour degradation event[18] |
| Google Weather API | Not independently benchmarked; refresh cadence 15-30 min | Rate limit of 6,000 queries/minute by default[19] |
| Weatherbit | Not independently benchmarked | Enterprise tier advertises a 200ms response SLA[11] |

Open-Meteo is architecturally built for speed, storing time-series data on NVMe disks specifically to minimize per-call latency, though real-world third-party measurements land closer to a few hundred milliseconds rather than the vendor's sub-10ms marketing figure. Only Weatherbit explicitly guarantees a latency SLA (200ms) and only on its priciest Enterprise plan.[11][14][16]

## Nowcasting Horizon and Radar Capability

| API | Nowcast Horizon | Update Frequency | Radar/Data Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tomorrow.io | 60-minute minute-by-minute precipitation (premium/Enterprise only)[20][21] | Radar+satellite composite refreshes every 5 minutes; proprietary "UP" blend refreshes every 30 seconds[22][23] | Proprietary microsatellite radar constellation + 1,000+ ground radar stations, 2.5km resolution[24][21] |
| Google Weather API | 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast (Experimental endpoint)[25] | Current/hourly data refreshed every 15-30 minutes[26][27] | Google explicitly states it does not do true nowcast/minute forecasting via traditional radar; the minute endpoint is AI-model based[19] |
| Visual Crossing | Minute-by-minute precipitation timing "when available" within its Weather Forecast Live tool[17] | Standard 15-day forecast; not a dedicated short-interval radar product[5] | Not radar-native; interpolation-based hyperlocal modeling[28] |
| Open-Meteo | 15-minutely data (Central Europe and North America only); hourly elsewhere via interpolation[8] | High-res regional models (ICON-D2, HRRR, AROME) update every 1-3 hours; global models every 6 hours[14] | No true radar-based nowcasting; model data only, no station observations[9] |
| Weatherbit | 60-minute minutely rain/snow nowcast[29][12] | Included from the Standard paid tier upward (not on Free)[11][30] | Blends stations, radar, and satellite globally[29] |

Tomorrow.io has the most genuinely radar-driven, sub-hour nowcast product in this group, with a proprietary satellite radar constellation designed to fill gaps where ground radar coverage is poor, and refresh rates as tight as 30 seconds to 5 minutes. Weatherbit offers a comparable 60-minute minutely product but only unlocks it once you leave the free tier. Google explicitly disclaims traditional nowcasting and instead offers an AI-modeled 6-hour minute-level precipitation forecast as an experimental endpoint, not classic radar extrapolation. Open-Meteo is the weakest here since it is pure numerical-model data with no radar ingestion, so true "rain starting in X minutes" nowcasting is out of scope.[12][25][24][19][22][23][9][11]

## Geographic Coverage

| API | Coverage Notes |
|---|---|
| Tomorrow.io | Global coverage claimed via NextGen satellite network, specifically marketed as filling North American radar gaps (27% of US landmass previously had poor radar quality)[24] |
| Google Weather API | Global except Japan, Korea (alerts-only), and a short list of excluded countries (China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria); initial launch also excludes remote unpopulated areas like open ocean and deserts[4][13][19] |
| Visual Crossing | Global coverage for both forecast and 50+ years of historical data[31] |
| Open-Meteo | Global, with highest resolution (1-2 km) in Central Europe, France, Switzerland, UK, and North America; 9-11 km elsewhere[14][9] |
| Weatherbit | Global coverage blending stations, radar, and satellite[29] |

Google is notably the most restrictive on paper, excluding a handful of countries outright and still ramping up quality in remote/unpopulated regions as of its post-GA rollout. Tomorrow.io and Open-Meteo both explicitly engineer around the reality that ground radar is unevenly distributed worldwide, but they solve it differently: Tomorrow.io launches its own radar satellites, while Open-Meteo simply uses the best available numerical model per region without radar at all.[13][14][24][19]

## Practical Takeaways

- **Best true nowcasting**: Tomorrow.io, thanks to its proprietary radar/satellite blend refreshed every 5 minutes to 30 seconds, though the best of it sits behind Enterprise pricing.[22][21]
- **Best budget/transparent pricing**: Open-Meteo and Visual Crossing, both with clear published per-call/per-record rates and no sales-call requirement.[5][9]
- **Best for low-latency simple forecasts**: Open-Meteo, if you don't need radar-based nowcasting and can tolerate its non-guaranteed uptime on the free tier.[14][9]
- **Best all-around SLA-backed option**: Weatherbit's Enterprise tier, the only one in this set with a published 200ms response-time SLA.[11]
- **Most cautious on global reach**: Google Weather API, due to explicit country exclusions and still-maturing remote-area coverage.[19][13]

## Further Knowledge

- Tomorrow.io's official comparison of its Unified Precipitation vs. Global Radar layers explains the tradeoffs between its two nowcasting data products.[22]
- Google's Weather API FAQ page details refresh cadence and explicitly addresses why it doesn't offer traditional nowcasting.[19]
- Open-Meteo's engineering blog post "How to store weather forecast data for fast time-series APIs" is a good technical read on how it achieves low-latency responses.[32]
- Visual Crossing's own blog post comparing its pricing model to the now-defunct Dark Sky API is useful context for understanding per-record billing.[33]
- APIbenchmarks' independent weather API leaderboard is a useful cross-check for documentation, reliability, and ecosystem scores beyond just price and latency.[34]
